# Cellwiser

Takes a set of Excel files plus a description of a manual workflow, reconstructs
that workflow as a machine-readable model, and **replays it as an animation on
top of an Excel-like grid**.

The deliverable is not a chatbot. It is the cell-level replay: a production
planner watches the process they run by hand play back on their own spreadsheets
and says either "yes, that's roughly what I do" or "no, you've got that bit
wrong" — and then corrects it through chat.

## Why it exists

A planner at a small manufacturer has 3–30 Excel files. Every day or every month
they read certain cells, apply rules that live in their head, and type results
into an output file. Nobody has written that process down. This reconstructs it,
and — importantly — is explicit about the parts it *cannot* reconstruct, because
those are the parts that only exist in the planner's experience.

That honesty is a first-class feature: `manual_judgment` is an operation type,
and `assumptions` / `unknowns` / `confidence` are mandatory on every step.

## Running it

```bash
npm install
cp .env.example .env.local   # set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
npm run dev
```

Then open http://localhost:3000 and press **Load sample** — or drop in your own
`.xlsx` / `.xlsm` / `.csv` files.

| Command | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `npm run dev` | Dev server on :3000 |
| `npm run check` | Typecheck + the full test suite |
| `npm test` | Unit tests only |
| `npm run check:inference` | Score a **real** model call against the conformance scenario (needs a key) |
| `npm run bench` | Score the pipeline against SpreadsheetBench 2 — see [docs/spreadsheetbench.md](docs/spreadsheetbench.md) |
| `npm run samples` | Regenerate `public/samples/` |
| `npm run scenario` | Regenerate `public/scenarios/` |

> Don't run `npm run build` while `npm run dev` is live — the production build
> overwrites the dev server's chunk manifest and the page goes blank with 404s
> on `main-app.js`. Stop dev, or `rm -rf .next` afterwards.

## Checking it actually works

There are two halves to be confident in, and they fail differently.

**The deterministic half** — parsing, digest, geometry. `public/scenarios/`
holds a workbook set where every feature is planted on purpose with a known
answer: a header pushed to row 3 by a title block, a merged cell, a cross-sheet
formula, two cross-file formulas, absolute anchors sitting next to relative
refs, a sheet with no header, and — the important one — two columns a human
types by hand with no formula anywhere in them.

`lib/scenario.ts` states the expected answer; `npm test` asserts the digest
finds all of it. Break formula normalisation and two tests go red.

**The model half** — does the reconstruction make sense? The schema only proves
the JSON is well-formed, so:

```bash
npm run check:inference          # one real call, scored
```

It runs the real prompt over the scenario and checks the result against the
planted facts: every range resolves to cells that exist, the tier lookup was
found, confidence is calibrated rather than flat, and above all that the two
hand-typed columns became a `manual_judgment` step with a question — not a
confidently invented approval rule. Exits non-zero on failure.

The grader is itself tested (`test/scenario-checks.test.ts`): each check is run
against a workflow that is correct by construction and against one broken in
exactly the way that check exists to catch.

**The external yardstick** — SpreadsheetBench 2. `npm run bench` runs the
whole stack — digest, model call, formula engine — against a public benchmark
of real business spreadsheet tasks and reports the official score (fraction
of tasks fully solved, with regression/modification breakdowns). The scoring
is a verified port of the official evaluator, and every run writes output
files the reference Python pipeline can re-score independently. Setup and
interpretation: [docs/spreadsheetbench.md](docs/spreadsheetbench.md).

You can also watch the scenario run end to end in the browser:

```
http://localhost:3000/?scenario=1
```

`public/scenarios/expected_workflow.json` is the reference answer to diff
against.

**Files never leave the browser.** Parsing happens client-side; only the digest
— headers, column shapes, and formula patterns — is sent to the API route, which
is the only place the Anthropic key is ever read.

### The pieces

| Path | Role |
| --- | --- |
| [`lib/ir/schema.ts`](lib/ir/schema.ts) | The IR. Everything else reads and writes this object. |
| [`lib/digest.ts`](lib/digest.ts) | Whole files → a <8k-token description. Formula patterns are the point. |
| [`lib/workbook.ts`](lib/workbook.ts) | SheetJS → a sparse grid model |
| [`lib/grid/geometry.ts`](lib/grid/geometry.ts) | Single source of truth for range geometry |
| [`lib/animation/player.ts`](lib/animation/player.ts) | One cancellable async routine driving the replay |
| [`components/grid/ExcelGrid.tsx`](components/grid/ExcelGrid.tsx) | Hand-built grid — four synced panes, virtualised |
| [`components/animation/AnimationLayer.tsx`](components/animation/AnimationLayer.tsx) | Read/transit/write overlay |

### Formula patterns

The digest normalises relative row refs so a filled-down column collapses to one
entry — 42 cells of `=E2-F2`, `=E3-F3`, … become:

```
K2:K43 (x42)  =E{r}-F{r}
```

Absolute anchors are preserved, because `$B$2` staying put while `A2` moves is
exactly what tells you which table is the authority.

## Notes and constraints

- **Model**: `claude-sonnet-4-6`. It has no structured-output mode, so JSON is
  enforced by prompt + Zod validation + one retry with the errors appended.
  Moving to `claude-sonnet-5` or `claude-opus-5` would make the schema
  API-enforced and demote the retry to a safety net.
- **SheetJS is installed from the vendor CDN**, not npm — the npm `xlsx` package
  is abandoned at 0.18.5 with unfixed prototype-pollution and ReDoS advisories.
  `npm install` therefore needs to reach `cdn.sheetjs.com`.
- **Caps**: 5,000 rows × 100 columns per sheet. Larger sheets render a banner
  saying what was hidden rather than silently truncating.

## Out of scope (v1)

Auth, persistence, multi-user, writing files back to disk, ERP connectors,
mobile layout, i18n.

# Vibehud — instructions for coding agents

This project uses **vibehud**: you (the agent) maintain `agent-map.md` at the
project root, and the app renders it live at `/vibehud` (dev only). The panel
validates your map against the real routes, so keep it truthful.

## When to update agent-map.md

Update the file **in the same turn** as the change it describes, whenever you:

1. Create, rename, or delete a page/route → update `pages` (and `relations`).
2. Create, rename, or delete an API route handler → update `apis` (path and
   methods).
3. Add or change a page's major building blocks (a form, a grid, a chart) →
   update that page's `elements`.
4. Integrate an external service or database → update `systems`.
4b. Build or change a backend pipeline whose steps are NOT routes (webhook
   processing, background jobs, emails, multi-step order handling) → declare
   it in `flows` with ordered `steps`, linking steps to pages/apis/systems
   via `uses` where they touch one. This is how hidden backend machinery
   stays visible and reviewable.
5. Start reading a new environment variable → add its NAME to `env` (never a
   value) and to `.env.example`.
6. Start, finish, or plan a piece of work → update `tasks` (todo/doing/done).
7. Are asked about progress → update the file first, then point the user to
   `/vibehud`.

If the panel shows "map drift" (missing or undeclared routes), fixing
`agent-map.md` is part of finishing your task.

**Verify with the CLI** — after updating the map, run:

```bash
npx vibehud check
```

Exit 0 means the map matches reality; exit 1 prints exactly what drifted
(`--json` for machine-readable output). Treat a failing check like a failing
test. Do NOT declare the `/vibehud` route itself — validation ignores it.

## File format

`agent-map.md` is markdown; the machine-readable part is one fenced block
tagged `yaml agent-map`:

```yaml agent-map
version: 1
app: "My App"
pages:
  - id: home
    label: Home
    path: /
    status: done
  - id: blog
    label: Blog
    path: /blog
    status: doing
    elements:
      - name: PostList
        kind: list
        status: done
      - name: SubscribeBox
        kind: form
        status: doing
apis:
  - id: subscribe-api
    label: Subscribe API
    path: /api/subscribe
    methods: [POST]
relations:
  - from: home
    to: blog
    type: nav
  - from: blog
    to: subscribe-api
    type: data
tasks:
  - id: t1
    title: "Write first post"
    status: todo
    page: blog
```

Field rules:

- `pages[]`: `id` (unique slug) and `path` required. `path` is the route as the
  router sees it, dynamic segments literal (`/blog/[slug]`). `status` is
  `todo` | `doing` | `done` (default `done`). Optional `elements` list what the
  page is made of (`name` required, optional `kind` and `status`) and an
  optional `note` shows in the detail panel.

# SpreadsheetBench 2 harness

`npm run bench` measures Cellwise's own pipeline — SheetJS parsing, the
digest, the schema-validated model call, and the TypeScript formula engine —
against [SpreadsheetBench 2](https://spreadsheetbench.github.io/)
([paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.29955)), a benchmark of 321 real business
spreadsheet tasks across four categories: `Debugging`, `Financial_Model`,
`Template`, and `Visualization`.

## Getting the dataset

The dataset is not bundled (it is several GB of real workbooks). Download it
once from [Hugging Face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/KAKA22/SpreadsheetBench-v2):

```bash
hf download KAKA22/SpreadsheetBench-v2 --repo-type dataset \
    --local-dir data/spreadsheetbench-v2
```

The runner looks in `data/spreadsheetbench-v2` by default; override with
`--dataset <dir>` or `SPREADSHEETBENCH_DIR`.

## Running

```bash
npm run bench -- --category Financial_Model --limit 5   # dip a toe (5 model calls)
npm run bench -- --category all                          # the full scoreable set
npm run bench -- --category Debugging --ids 3,17         # specific tasks
npm run bench -- --category Template --baseline          # no model calls: the floor
npm run bench -- --category all --concurrency 4 --resume # restartable long run
npm run bench -- --category Template --score-only <dir>  # score any {id}_output.xlsx set
```

Each task is one model call (`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` required except in
`--baseline` / `--score-only`). `--resume` skips tasks whose output file
already exists and scores it from disk, so an interrupted run continues
where it stopped.

## Modes

`--mode tools` (default) runs each task as an agentic loop: the model gets
the budget-honest digest and grid listing up front, plus retrieval tools —
`read_range`, `search_cells`, `trace_cell`, `lookup_defined_names` — and
finishes by calling `submit_edit_plan`. Submitted plans are validated and
evaluated through the formula engine before acceptance; evaluation errors
(#NAME?, parse failures) are fed back once so the model can correct them.
Caps: 12 assistant turns / 40 tool calls per task, then the task falls back
to the standard planError scoring (unchanged input).

`--mode single` is the pre-tools single-shot path, kept for A/B comparison:
one prompt, one validated JSON response, one retry on validation failure.

Per-task diagnostics in `report.json` gain `turns`, `toolCalls`,
`submitOutcome` (`clean | warned | capped | planError`) and `cacheRead`
tokens in tools mode.

## What a run does

For every task the harness:

1. parses the input workbook (`lib/workbook.ts`) and builds the same digest
   the app sends to `/api/infer` (`lib/digest.ts`), plus a budgeted grid
   listing of actual cell contents;
2. asks the model for an **edit plan** — concrete cell edits (formula /
   value / grid / clear per range), validated with Zod against the actual
   workbook so a typo'd sheet or range is fed back for one correction, the
   same loop the workflow IR uses;
3. applies the plan through the formula engine (`lib/formula/simulate.ts`):
   new formulas are parsed, wired into the dependency graph, filled across
   ranges with Excel's relative-reference semantics (`lib/formula/shift.ts`),
   and the workbook recalculates. Only cells inside the edits' blast radius
   (edited, or downstream of an edit in the dependency graph) take engine
   values; untouched cells keep the file's own Excel-computed cached values,
   so an engine/Excel disagreement on a cell no edit reached is never scored
   as damage the plan did;
4. scores the result against the golden file with a verified port of the
   official evaluator (`lib/bench/compare.ts`), and writes
   `<out>/<Category>/output_excel/{id}_output.xlsx` — the exact layout the
   official Python evaluator consumes, so any run can be independently
   re-scored with the reference pipeline.

The model never sees `answer_position` (the scored ranges) — the same
information boundary the official harness gives its agents.

## Reading the score

Cells named by a task's `answer_position` split into **regression** cells
(identical in input and golden — the task must not disturb them) and
**modification** cells (changed by the golden answer — the task must produce
them). Per task:

- `regressionAccuracy` — fraction of regression cells preserved; ≥ 99.8%
  counts as 1.0 (official rule);
- `modificationAccuracy` — fraction of modification cells correct, under 1%
  numeric tolerance, date-serial equivalence, `#N/A`-style placeholder
  equivalence, and case/anchor-insensitive formula comparison;
- `accuracy` — 1 only when both of the above are 1.0.

The headline number — the one comparable to the paper's leaderboard — is the
mean `accuracy`: the fraction of tasks fully solved. `report.json` in each
category's results folder carries per-task detail: what was edited, the first
mismatching cell, formulas the engine could not parse, and functions outside
the registry (`#NAME?`).

Comparison semantics are locked to the reference implementation by a
differential test (5,408 value/formula pairs through both the official
`compare_cell_value`/`compare_cell_formula` and this port — zero mismatches)
and by running the official `evaluation.py` on harness-produced output files.

## Known limitations

- **Visualization tasks are not attempted.** They are judged on rendered
  charts by a VLM (on Windows, over Excel COM) in the official pipeline, and
  Cellwise has no charting.
- **Font-color checks are skipped** on Debugging tasks whose path contains
  `Color` — SheetJS CE does not reliably expose per-cell font colors. Those
  tasks are scored on values and flagged `fontColorSkipped` in the report;
  the official evaluator remains the authority for that slice.
- **The app's 5,000×100 grid cap does not apply to scoring.** The benchmark
  parses workbooks at Excel's own maxima (251 sheets in the dataset exceed
  100 columns), so the engine and the scorer see whole sheets; only the
  structural digest is built from an app-capped parse, with the budgeted
  grid appendix carrying full-size content to the model. A sheet that still
  overflows is flagged `TRUNCATED` rather than silently mis-scored.
- **The engine's function registry is the ceiling.** A golden answer needing
  a function outside the ~105 supported ones can only be matched by a
  precomputed value; the prompt says so and the report counts every
  `#NAME?`. This is a feature: the benchmark exists to show where the
  engine's coverage ends.
- Formula-mode comparison (Debugging `Embedded` tasks) compares the formulas
  the plan wrote; number-format-only changes are invisible to it, as they
  are to the official evaluator.

# Layered file analysis: budget-honest digest + an agentic tool loop

Date: 2026-08-15

## The problem

The first real SpreadsheetBench 2 model run died before spending a token:
`Financial_Model/01_01` produced a **1,175,117-token prompt** against the
API's 1,000,000 ceiling. Measured breakdown (probe on the real file):

```
definedNames   1,610,836 chars  (~450k tok)  10,739 names, mostly legacy junk
sheet sections   289,973 chars  (~80k tok)   per-column stats × 25 sheets, up to 165 cols
grid appendix    135,341 chars  (~38k tok)   budgeted (minor ~13% overshoot)
everything else     small
```

`buildFileDigest` ([lib/digest.ts](../../../lib/digest.ts)) has a 8,000-token
budget and five shrink plans — but the plans only shrink `sampleRows` and
`formulaPatterns`, the two *smallest* fields. `definedNames` and `sections`
are never touched, so for a workbook shaped like a real 20-year-old financial
model the budget is fiction: the tightest plan still emits **554k tokens** and
the code ships it anyway. Any Cellwise user could upload this same file
tomorrow; this is a product bug the benchmark happened to catch first.

## Decisions taken (with the user)

- **Staging:** Stage 1 fixes the budget and produces a scored single-shot
  baseline; Stage 2 builds the layered tool architecture and must beat that
  baseline. Both stages ship; neither is skipped.
- **Stage 2 scope:** bench-first. The analysis tools are built as shared
  library code; the benchmark runner is the first consumer. `/api/infer`
  adoption is a follow-up project, not part of this one.
- **Interaction shape:** Approach B — rich budget-honest context up front
  *plus* retrieval tools for what the budget cut, with a strict terminal
  submit tool. Chosen over a pure agentic explorer (overhead on easy tasks,
  bigger behavioral leap from the measured baseline) and a two-phase scripted
  pipeline (no recovery, no reusable tool surface).
- **Model:** `claude-sonnet-5` (already the pinned `MODEL`), effort via the
  existing `--effort` flag.

## Stage 1 — `buildFileDigest` honors its budget, always

**Contract:** `buildFileDigest(wb, budget)` never returns a digest whose
estimate exceeds `budget`, for any input workbook.

Changes in [lib/digest.ts](../../../lib/digest.ts):

1. **Defined names: ranked, filtered, capped.** Render priority: names
   referenced by the workbook's formulas first, then valid-ref names, then
   the rest; junk refs (array literals, `#REF!`) always last. Cap by plan:
   200 → 100 → 50 → 25 → 10. Always emit one note line with the omitted
   count (`10,539 more defined names omitted`) so the model knows they exist
   and can retrieve them (Stage 2's `lookup_defined_names`).
2. **Sections join the shrink plans.** New per-plan `sectionColumns`
   dimension (60 → 40 → 25 → 12 → 6 columns per sheet), truncation noted
   per sheet.
3. **Hard floor after the tightest plan.** Degrade in order: drop sample
   rows → drop formula-pattern examples → shrink per-sheet detail
   proportionally, largest sheets first. Never dropped: the complete sheet
   list (names + dimensions) and the notes recording what was cut. A final
   explicit check enforces the post-condition; if somehow still over, the
   rendered form is truncated with a note — never shipped 70× over budget.
4. **Grid appendix share fix (minor):** the per-sheet floor
   (`min(4000, budget/sheets) × 25 sheets` plus weighted shares) can
   overshoot the 120k-char budget by ~13%. Normalize shares so the total
   respects the budget.

Not changed in Stage 1: prompts, model, scoring, the app's inference route.
Existing digest tests pass untouched (fixtures never hit the caps); new
tests cover caps and floor.

**Immediately after landing:** re-run `01_01` (expected ~50k input tokens,
was 1.17M), then `Financial_Model --limit 10` — the single-shot baseline.

# Spreadsheet analysis harness

A standalone copy of the spreadsheet-analysis engine from
[WhemDev/cellwiser](https://github.com/WhemDev/cellwiser) (commit `e88d886`),
with the Next.js app, database, auth and UI removed. What's left is the part
that **reads Excel workbooks, describes them to an LLM, lets the LLM explore
and edit them through tools, recalculates the result with a real formula
engine, and scores it**.

You can use it in three ways:

1. **As a library.** Parse `.xlsx` files, get a compact, token-budgeted
   summary of them, query cells, trace formulas, and run what-if
   recalculations. No API key needed.
2. **As an agent harness.** Give Claude a workbook and a task. It reads the
   digest, calls retrieval tools (`read_range`, `search_cells`, `trace_cell`,
   `lookup_defined_names`) and submits an edit plan. The harness validates the
   plan and evaluates it through the formula engine before accepting it.
3. **As a benchmark runner.** Score the whole pipeline against
   [SpreadsheetBench 2](https://spreadsheetbench.github.io/) (321 real
   business spreadsheet tasks), using a verified port of the official
   evaluator.

---

## Quick start

```bash
cd spreadsheet-harness
npm install          # needs network access to cdn.sheetjs.com (see Notes)
npm run example      # model-free tour on a bundled sample workbook
npm run check        # typecheck + ~2,800 unit tests
```

`npm run example` runs [`examples/analyze.ts`](examples/analyze.ts). Its
output looks like this:

```
# capacity.xlsx: 2 sheet(s), digest ≈ 1266 tokens
- Work Centers: 2 formula pattern(s)
    G2:G7 (x6)  =C{r}*D{r}*E{r}*F{r}
    I2:I7 (x6)  =G{r}*H{r}
...
what-if: WORK CENTERS!C2 := 0 → Work Centers!G2 150 → 0
```

To run it on your own file:

```bash
npx tsx examples/analyze.ts path/to/your.xlsx
```

---

## How it works

```
 .xlsx bytes
     │
     ▼
 parseWorkbook ──► ParsedWorkbook (sparse grid: values, formulas, styles, names)
     │                    │
     │                    ├──► createSimulator ──► formula engine (dependency graph,
     │                    │                        ~105 Excel functions, recalc)
     ▼                    │
 buildFileDigest          │
 (≤ 8k tokens/file)       │
     │                    │
     ▼                    ▼
 prompt + grid appendix ──► runAgentLoop ──► Claude
                               ▲   │  tool calls: read_range / search_cells /
                               │   │              trace_cell / lookup_defined_names
                               │   ▼
                               └── submit_edit_plan ──► validate (Zod, against the
                                                        real workbook) ──► apply through
                                                        the engine ──► feedback once
                                                                │
                                                                ▼
                                                  buildOutputXlsx ──► output .xlsx
                                                                │
                                                                ▼
                                                  compare.ts ──► score vs golden
```

The main design ideas:

- **The digest always fits its budget.** Real financial models can have more
  than 10,000 defined names and hundreds of columns. The digest ranks and caps
  them, tightens through a series of shrink plans, and adds a note for
  everything it left out, so the model knows to fetch it with a tool. It never
  sends more than the token budget.
- **Formula patterns are collapsed.** 42 cells of `=E2-F2`, `=E3-F3`, … become
  one line, `K2:K43 (x42) =E{r}-F{r}`. Absolute anchors such as `$B$2` are
  kept, because they show which table is the source of truth.
- **The model's edits are checked before they're accepted.** An edit plan is
  validated against the actual sheets and ranges, then executed in the formula
  engine. Errors like `#NAME?` or parse failures are sent back to the model so
  it can correct them.
- **Only cells affected by an edit take engine values.** Cells that no edit
  reached keep the values Excel cached in the file. That way, a place where
  the engine and Excel disagree is never counted as damage done by the plan.

---

## Folder map

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| [`lib/workbook.ts`](lib/workbook.ts) | SheetJS → `ParsedWorkbook` (sparse grid). `parseWorkbook(bytes, name, limits?)` |
| [`lib/workbook-styles.ts`](lib/workbook-styles.ts) | Reads cell styles/number formats from the raw xlsx |
| [`lib/digest.ts`](lib/digest.ts) | `buildFileDigest(wb, budget)`: headers, column types, sections, repeated blocks, period axes, formula patterns |
| [`lib/analysis/`](lib/analysis/) | Retrieval tools (`readRange`, `searchCells`, `traceCell`, `lookupDefinedNames`), completeness checks, formula-outlier detection |
| [`lib/agent/`](lib/agent/) | The agent loop (`runAgentLoop`), tool definitions, grid appendix, restraint/axis checks on submitted plans |
| [`lib/formula/`](lib/formula/) | TypeScript Excel formula engine: tokenizer → parser → AST → evaluator, dependency graph, fill/shift, `createSimulator` |
| [`lib/plan/`](lib/plan/) | Edit-plan schema (`makeEditPlanSchema`), `applyEditPlan`, `buildOutputXlsx` (write result back to .xlsx) |
| [`lib/charts/`](lib/charts/) | Chart spec → DrawingML compiler and xlsx injection (for Visualization tasks) |
| [`lib/anthropic/`](lib/anthropic/) | Anthropic client (`MODEL = claude-sonnet-5`), validated JSON calls with one retry |
| [`lib/bedrock/`](lib/bedrock/) | Optional AWS Bedrock backend for the same agent loop |
| [`lib/bench/`](lib/bench/) | SpreadsheetBench 2: dataset parsing, prompts, per-task runner, scorer (`compare.ts`), logs |
| [`lib/ir/schema.ts`](lib/ir/schema.ts) | Shared Zod types the prompts and plans reference |
| [`scripts/benchmark.ts`](scripts/benchmark.ts) | `npm run bench`: the benchmark CLI |
| [`scripts/bench-digest-sweep.ts`](scripts/bench-digest-sweep.ts) | Measure digest size across the dataset (no model calls) |
| [`scripts/bench-dry-score.ts`](scripts/bench-dry-score.ts) | Score without a model (sanity check of the scorer) |
| [`simulation/`](simulation/) + [`scripts/dump-oracle.py`](scripts/dump-oracle.py) | Python reference formula engine used to generate the oracle fixtures the TS engine is tested against |
| [`public/samples/`](public/samples/), [`public/scenarios/`](public/scenarios/) | Small synthetic workbooks used by tests and the example |
| [`test/`](test/) | Vitest suites for everything above |
| [`docs/`](docs/) | Upstream design notes: benchmark guide, status/handoff, Bedrock guide, layered-analysis design |

---

## Using it as a library

```ts
import { readFileSync } from "node:fs";
import { parseWorkbook } from "./lib/workbook";
import { buildFileDigest } from "./lib/digest";
import { readRange, searchCells, traceCell, lookupDefinedNames } from "./lib/analysis/tools";
import { createSimulator } from "./lib/formula/simulate";

const wb = parseWorkbook(new Uint8Array(readFileSync("model.xlsx")), "model.xlsx");

const digest = buildFileDigest(wb);              // compact JSON summary, ≤ 8k tokens
readRange(wb, "Sheet1", "A1:H20").text;          // cell contents as text (formula -> value)
searchCells(wb, "revenue", { limit: 20 });       // where does a label/value appear?

const sim = createSimulator(wb);                 // live formula engine over the workbook
traceCell(sim, "Sheet1", "H20", "precedents");   // what feeds this cell?
await sim.setValue("Inputs", "B3", 0.25);        // what-if
await sim.recalculate();
sim.getValue("Sheet1", "H20");
```

To keep big files intact for full analysis, pass larger parse limits. By
default, sheets are capped at 5,000 rows × 100 columns; the benchmark uses
Excel's full maxima:

```ts
import { BENCH_PARSE_LIMITS } from "./lib/bench/run-task";
parseWorkbook(bytes, name, BENCH_PARSE_LIMITS); // 1,048,576 × 16,384
```

## Using it as an agent harness

[`lib/bench/run-task.ts`](lib/bench/run-task.ts) (`runBenchTask`) runs one
task from start to finish, and you inject the model call. That makes it the
easiest place to start wiring the harness into your own agent: reuse
`runAgentLoop` from [`lib/agent/loop.ts`](lib/agent/loop.ts) with the tool set
from [`lib/agent/tools.ts`](lib/agent/tools.ts), and swap the benchmark prompt
in [`lib/bench/prompts.ts`](lib/bench/prompts.ts) for your own task
description. Limits: 12 assistant turns and 40 tool calls per task.

Tests drive the loop with a stubbed model, so you can try new tools or prompts
without spending tokens. See
[`test/bench-agent-loop.test.ts`](test/bench-agent-loop.test.ts) and
[`test/bench-run-task.test.ts`](test/bench-run-task.test.ts).

## Running the benchmark

```bash
cp .env.example .env.local            # fill in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY
set -a; source .env.local; set +a

# one-time dataset download (several GB, kept out of git via .gitignore)
hf download KAKA22/SpreadsheetBench-v2 --repo-type dataset --local-dir data/spreadsheetbench-v2

npm run bench -- --category Template --baseline          # free: no model calls, shows the floor
npm run bench -- --category Financial_Model --limit 5    # 5 real tasks
npm run bench -- --category all --concurrency 4 --resume # full, restartable run
```

Results go to `bench-results/<Category>/`. Each category gets a
`report.json` with per-task details, plus `output_excel/{id}_output.xlsx` in
the layout the official Python evaluator reads. Run
`npx tsx scripts/benchmark.ts` for the full flag list (`--mode tools|single`,
`--effort`, `--model`, `--provider bedrock`, `--score-only`, …). For how to
read the score, see [docs/spreadsheetbench.md](docs/spreadsheetbench.md).

---

## Notes

- **SheetJS is installed from its vendor CDN** (`cdn.sheetjs.com`), not npm.
  The npm `xlsx` package is abandoned at 0.18.5 and has open security
  advisories.
- **The engine supports about 105 Excel functions.** Anything outside that set
  evaluates to `#NAME?`, and the benchmark report counts these.
- **Known failing tests:** 2 tests in `test/digest-period-axis.test.ts` (the
  monthly/annual period-axis grouping) fail. They fail the same way in
  upstream cellwiser at `e88d886`, so this extraction didn't cause them. The
  rest pass: 2,815 passed and 16 skipped (skipped suites need the downloaded
  dataset or a private `Excaliba.xlsx` workbook).
- **Not included:** the Next.js UI, the animation player, the Works/runs
  store, Supabase, auth/metering, and the workflow-IR inference routes. For
  those, see the upstream repo.
- **Syncing with upstream:** this is a one-time copy, not a submodule. To
  pick up upstream changes, re-copy the matching paths from `WhemDev/cellwiser`
  (every file here keeps its original path).
